title: Satyakama at the teacher's door
hookLine: a boy asks his mother who his father was; she doesn't know, and he carries that answer, word for word, to his teacher
tomorrow: the bull, the fire, the swan, the bird
last: BHAVA: THE CHANT NEEDS ITS INSIDE.

cards: Name. Date of birth. Father's name.

On plenty of old forms, that third line sat near the top, and for some people it was the hardest line on the page. In the Chandogya, a boy who wants to study the Veda faces the spoken version of that line.
A teacher will ask: what is your family, your lineage? So the boy, Satyakama, goes home first and asks his mother.

teach.b: His mother's name is Jabala, and she answers him honestly. I don't know your lineage, my son. When I was young, I moved about a great deal working as a servant, and that's when I had you.
But I am Jabala, and you are Satyakama. So call yourself Satyakama Jabala: a name made from his mother, not his father.

teach.h: HE REPEATS IT ALL TO THE TEACHER.
teach.b: The boy walks to the teacher, Haridrumata Gautama, and asks to become his student. The teacher asks: what is your lineage, my dear?
And Satyakama repeats his mother's words, all of them, the part that might shame her and the part that might shut him out. I don't know, sir.
My mother says she moved about as a servant when she was young, and had me then. She is Jabala, I am Satyakama. I'm Satyakama Jabala.
The teacher's reply is the hinge of the story. No one but a true brahmin could speak like that, he says. Fetch the firewood, my dear.
I'll take you as a student.

teach.h: YOU HAVE NOT GONE FROM THE TRUTH.
teach.b: You have not gone away from the truth. Look at what counts as the qualification here. Not birth.
Not a well-known father. The truth, told when a lie would have been easier.
His very name holds it: satya means truth, kama means desire. Satyakama, the one who loves truth. Hindus have read this story in different ways.

For some, it shows that character is what a brahmin really is. Others, including some traditional commentators, read the teacher as concluding that a boy this truthful must be of brahmin birth after all.
Either way, the story keeps the boy at the door, saying I don't know, out loud.

how: Satyakama's story is told to Hindu children as a lesson in honesty, and teachers cite it when discussing whether spiritual standing comes from birth or from character.

o: a mother who raised her son working as a servant
one who loves truth: the honest boy at the door
the teacher who accepts a new student

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: you are accepted as a student

s: Satyakama made up a respectable lineage to be accepted
he repeated his mother's words exactly: I don't know.
he takes his name from his mother
the teacher accepts him because he didn't go away from the truth
telling the truth at the door is the qualification.

games.q: you're Satyakama at the teacher's door. he asks your lineage. your mother has told you she doesn't know who your father is. what do you say?
o: invent a father from a good family.
repeat exactly what your mother told you.
change the subject and ask about the lessons.
games.why: he tells it all, word for word. the teacher says only a true brahmin speaks like that, and tells him to fetch the firewood.

practice: Settle into the breath and think of one true thing about yourself that you usually leave out: something you don't know, something you aren't, a part of your story you skip.
You don't have to tell anyone; just let it be true here, without dressing it up or explaining it away. Notice whether it feels heavier hidden, or lighter said.

wordCard.voice: Satyakama. The one who loves truth: a boy without a known father, accepted as a student because he told the truth at the door.

orig.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, what really is. Satyakāma: one who desires truth.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, truth is the qualification. A boy with no lineage to give had exactly that. See you tomorrow.
